title: A Little The Crucible . A Little The Craft . A Lot of Catholic Guilt.
excerpt: The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school
body: The new Netflix show’s title card bears its name in a Gothic typeface—fittingly monastic for a series set in a Catholic high school

But upon closer look, the imposing script is specifically referencing a more modern aesthetic: the rhinestone-studded Juicy Couture logo, frequently seen in the early aughts emblazoned across the backsides of velour tracksuits

That choice, however, is startlingly apropos: The Body , set in 2004, is as much concerned with girlhood—and all of its material obsessions and hormonal impulses—as it is with the religious experience
Here, in fact, these often seem to be considered one and the same

The show, a mix of campy horror and psychodrama, has topped the streaming charts; it has also earned the ire of some viewers who consider its premise blasphemous—the story of a Catholic school’s girls’ dance team called the Lions, whose members reckon with their beliefs in the fallout of a traumatic event: In the series premiere, the teens lead an Ecstasy-powered, mock-satanic hazing ritual at a Halloween party, after which one new member, Grace (played by Sofia Wylie), has several seizures
She then dies but somehow comes back to life—what one girl drolly describes as a Jesus-like resurrection

As Grace lies comatose, her teammates question whether her condition is the result of Satan preying on them for invoking his name during the initiation, and whether the “visions” they each start having are the result of mass hysteria; the series makes a valid case for both possibilities
The Body revels in the teens’ more garden-variety exploits as well, in explicit scenes (back-seat sex, raunchy drawings) that are par for the course with today’s teen dramas

The difference here, however, is that this show often depicts messing with drugs and messing with the devil as equally dangerous adolescent acts of rebellion. [ Read: The Americans having the most sex ] Most of the Lions initially treat Catholicism as a joke, and they want everyone else to see them laughing
One girl sports a tight-fitting T-shirt that reads Jesus saves
Before the Halloween party, the co-captain Elise (Sara Boustany) warns the other dancers that donning provocative schoolgirl costumes is “redundant.” The event itself is held at what the St
Mark’s students call the “Devil’s House,” an abandoned convent whose former inhabitants are rumored to have lost their minds
The night offers the teens a chance to flip a symbolic middle finger to a religious institution that demands their subservience
Defiance is a form of self-control, and they exercise it in the most extreme ways possible
But after Grace seemingly begins to haunt her teammates, the girls’ faith takes on a visceral—even punishing—quality
Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the outsider classmate who once spoke in tongues before forcing her way on to the dance team, encourages the teens’ mounting fears of divine persecution
In response, they each begin confessing their sins, religious and social. (“I made out with Katie’s dad!” one of them admits

Another shouts that she’s “part of the fucking chess club!”) What’s really pouring out in these girls’ revelations, however, is all of the pent-up steam that can accumulate for a teen stuck in a Catholic-school hothouse
The girls have long been fed a diet of mixed messages when it comes to their physical and emotional selves
Their teachers tell them that their bodies are temples they should keep pure
Pop culture, meanwhile, tells them that their bodies are tools of pleasure
They’ve been raised in the era of postfeminist girl power —the Spice Girls likely soundtracked their elementary-school years—and absorbed the notion that their destiny is theirs to control
But their faith, in the show’s rendering, still shoves women toward the back
It’s no wonder that when the Lions begin to suspect that they can directly affect their own lives, they crack
Their identities, the show seems to argue, are inextricable from the rules, rituals, and cultural influences that dominate their lives
The Body , then, works as a study in what happens when young women break from the strictures that keep them in line
These characters feel as ecstatic as saints and as tortured as martyrs, sometimes in the same hour—being a teenage girl has room for all expressions of faith.

title: This Thanksgiving, I’m Grateful for Claude
excerpt: It used to be that on a typical afternoon, my husband would send me a message asking whether he needed to grab anything for dinner on his way home from work
body: It used to be that on a typical afternoon, my husband would send me a message asking whether he needed to grab anything for dinner on his way home from work
Ah, dinner . “What do we eat?” I would say. “Well, there’s always fajitas,” he’d suggest. “Or I guess we could do tortellini again,” I’d offer

Or maybe one of us would say, half-heartedly, that we should try something new. (Cue some Googling for easy family-dinner recipes .) On our best days, this conversation would occur midday, leaving time for a fridge check
More often, it would occur at 5:15 p.m. while I was standing on the sidelines of my kids’ swimming lesson or supervising a playground trip, straining to remember whether we already had mozzarella
Hours later, and about 13 minutes before bedtime was theoretically supposed to begin, we’d all sit down to a hastily prepared meal

Repeated over years, this quotidian ritual started to become agonizing—so much so that I empathized deeply with the author of an essay published last year in The New York Times , headlined “ Why I Had to Kill Family Dinner .” My own mom and dad—the parents of five children —eventually did just that, slipping into a “fend for yourselves” system on most nights by the time I was a preteen
My husband and I, though, were desperate to avoid such an outcome
For one thing, I really enjoy cooking, as does he; it’s not a task we want to abandon entirely
Contingent on having all of the requisite ingredients in front of us, we like messing around and trying new recipes too
The trouble is, we struggle to reliably ensure that the ingredients are, in fact, in front of us
It’s the planning—the “mental load,” as they say—that isn’t happening
For another, my husband and I want to be the sort of couple who can regularly host people for dinner, a pastime that’s been receding from American life

The share of people in the United States who’ve given or attended a dinner party at least once in the past year fell from 70 percent to 57 percent over the past three decades; just 12 percent of Americans host friends or family monthly, down a whopping 70 percent since 1975
Yet despite our best intentions, my husband and I rarely have our stuff together enough to host
This means that we tend to mooch our way through shared festivities, readily showing up wherever we’re invited but finding it a struggle to reciprocate on our own turf
So when I started seeing posts online from parents describing the ways that AI is revolutionizing their meal planning, I was intrigued
Like many people, I have grave concerns about artificial intelligence and what it means for the future of humanity
I worry that even if AI doesn’t lead to our extinction, it will further erode the human element from our lives and drive us deeper into isolation

But when it comes to dinner, I realized, AI might have the potential to move the needle in the other direction—to ease the logistical burden of meal planning and, in doing so, help people find their way back to one another
I’ve spent a lot of time reflecting on why my husband and I find such a simple task—choosing what to feed people—so difficult
And I’ve landed on a few reasons: First, before you can pick what’s for dinner, you’ve got to be able to remember what your options are
We’ve never developed a good system for this

I can’t tell you the number of times we’ve tried a recipe, loved it, and said “We need to add that into the rotation” only for that recipe to be almost immediately forgotten in the graveyard of bookmarked recipes spread across our digital devices
Beyond that, our mutual lack of strong preferences can be a real disadvantage
We learned this lesson the hard way while planning our wedding
I assumed, naively, that being the sort of person who didn’t care whether we ate chicken or salmon would be an asset
The ability to shrug one’s shoulders at any given outcome is helpful only when you are not the one making a decision
This of course applies to family dinner: You have to make a choice, not only for yourself but also on behalf of everyone in attendance
Its capacity for recalling every protein-rich meal our kids enjoy that might be suitable for a cold week in November is limitless
So, several weeks ago, I decided to see whether it could simply take over the task of meal planning entirely
We use Claude, and I fed it a document listing several recipes that my family likes or that I had a hunch we’d like, along with our lunch and breakfast staples
I told it that we’re a family of five and appreciate having leftovers
Then I asked it to pick five dinners and make a grocery list
It sounds sort of silly, but: We made dinner easily every night and ate it together
Because we were choosing from a short list of meals for which we already had the ingredients, we didn’t agonize over what to cook

And because two of those meals resulted in leftovers, we entered the weekend with everything ready for dinner Saturday night, which I’m pretty sure is a family first—one with unanticipated prosocial consequences
We were already planning to meet my sister and her family at a festival around the corner from our home that day
And in the fridge and pantry, we had all that we needed for a Tuscan chicken pasta
After the fest, we invited everyone to our house
Week 2 was a true test of our new system: My husband was out of town, which left me alone with the three kids

title: Measles, MAHA, and the Future of Disease in America
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Updated at 9:35 a.m
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Updated at 9:35 a.m
ET on November 26, 2026 The measles are back
The U.S. achieved measles-elimination status back in 2000 and then lost it earlier this month
To date, there have been more than 40 outbreaks and 5,800 cases since the year began, according to the CDC data—a significant jump from the 2,289 confirmed cases last year
Such an outbreak is exactly the sort of thing lawmakers who questioned Robert F

Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vaccine activism during his confirmation hearings had been worried about. “Frankly, you frighten people,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said at the time, before urging Kennedy to promise “never to say vaccines aren’t medically safe when they in fact are.” Since the measles-elimination status was removed, Kennedy has argued that Americans need to work to rebuild trust in vaccines

As the Make America Healthy Again movement comes face-to-face with the dangers of abjuring scientific consensus, my colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss an outstanding question: Where do we go from here? The following is a transcript of the episode: Tom Bartlett: Most people in this country are in favor of vaccination—Democrats, Republicans
We’re actually not that polarized on that issue
What we have is a very vocal group of people, including Robert F
Kennedy Jr., who have been pushing this contrarian and erroneous message about the dangers of vaccines for a long time
But if you get to the point where you have parents sort of forgoing normal childhood immunization, yeah, we should be worried. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic
I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to talk about measles and MAHA
During his confirmation hearing to become the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services in 2025, Robert F
Kennedy Jr.: I wanna thank President Trump for entrusting me to deliver on his promise to make America healthy again
Harris: But last week, after nearly three decades, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States has lost its measles-elimination status
Measles was eliminated back in 2000 because people were getting their shots, but in recent years, vaccination rates have fallen as misinformation about their safety has proliferated

When the elimination status was removed, Kennedy Jr. said, quote, “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust.” But many scientists and doctors argue Kennedy, a noted vaccine skeptic, is a large part of the reason why that trust was broken in the first place
What does it mean that measles are back? And where does the movement to make America healthy again go from here? My colleague Tom Bartlett joins me to discuss
Harris: I wanna start with a basic question

How did we get here? What does it mean that the U.S. has lost its measles-elimination status? Bartlett: In technical terms, it means that we’ve had at least 12 months where a single strain has been transmitted throughout the country
And so you have this essentially unbroken stretch where people have been getting the measles
So that’s sort of the technical definition
But I mean, I think measles is now—it was ruled eliminated in 2000, which means there were still sporadic outbreaks, but it was basically under control
And so losing that elimination status is really a sign that it’s really no longer in control, and that there’s this work to be done

In terms of how we got here, I think the key thing that people point to is pandemic disruption in vaccination schedules and areas where that vaccination rate among kindergartners fell below 95 percent, which is the herd-immunity threshold
So that’s kind of the basics of why we’re here

Harris: I guess how big of a deal is it that we’ve lost the status? If it’s sort of moving from sporadic to a sort of continuous strain of infections, is this, like, COVID-size, or what’s the scale that we’re thinking of here? Bartlett: So right now, these infections have been mostly confined to severely undervaccinated communities
So it’s a lot of Mennonite communities and Amish communities
And for the most part, that’s where it stayed
And so, are we looking at COVID-wide outbreaks? I think the short answer is no, but we also just don’t know where this ends, how much bigger this gets
We do have undervaccinated areas of the country that aren’t predominantly Mennonite or Amish
They haven’t, for the most part, been affected significantly
But I think we don’t know where this ends
And then just in general, it’s a sign that something needs to be done, a vaccination push or something, because it’s no longer eliminated
We thought we were moving toward eradication, which would be: We don’t have any outbreaks at all, even sporadic ones
So it’s really a sign that we’ve taken a step back, and that’s not what we would hope to do from a public-health point of view

Harris: I think most people don’t necessarily have a context for measles at this point, or if they do, it’s so far removed, and we can talk about it in terms of the numbers, but there is a real sort of human impact to this
These are families who are experiencing the loss of loved ones
You’ve done a lot of reporting in these communities
Can you sort of humanize this a little bit for folks? What are these families going through? Bartlett: Yeah, you’re right

title: The Scandinavian Compromise
excerpt: We live in a divided nation, and for at least the next two years, we’re going to have a divided government, with one party in control of Congress and the other
body: We live in a divided nation, and for at least the next two years, we’re going to have a divided government, with one party in control of Congress and the other in control of the White House
But never fear: I am here to bring us together
I think I’ve found a model that I believe will give people on the right and the left what they want
And, unusually for a former Wall Street Journal editorial page writer, I’m looking to Scandinavia for inspiration
As Brink Lindsey argues in his book The Permanent Problem , the two big challenges we face are inclusion and dynamism
It’s possible to get distracted by the current arguments about the exact nature of America’s class divide
Progressives emphasize how much wealth is going to the top one percent
People like me emphasize that the top 20 percent has created a caste system separating the highly educated, who rig everything to their benefit, from everybody else, who are left with the scraps
The truth is that both kinds of inequality are terrible
Great nations decline when they become grossly unequal, and America is staring that possibility straight in the face
Yes, it’s true that over the course of this century the American economy has enormously outperformed the economies of Germany, France, Britain, and Japan
But you get no prizes for besting those geezers
The fact is that for the past 50 years, America’s economic growth and productivity numbers have been sluggish and disappointing
This loss of economic dynamism has retarded wage growth, led to fiscal crises, and contributed to a decline in social mobility

In her forthcoming book, Reviving the American Dream , the Brookings Institution economist Isabel Sawhill notes that if America had sustained the productivity growth levels we enjoyed from 1948 to 1973, and if wages had kept pace with productivity, then the average annual earnings for a 25-to-54-year-old worker would be close to $180,000 a year
Instead, we’re living in a country in which the average wage is less than $70,000 a year
The psychological effect of these two crises is devastating—loss of trust, pessimism, alienation, class resentment, and pervasive economic insecurity
Historically, responsibility for these two problems has been divided between the major parties
Republicans were the party of dynamism, emphasizing tax cuts, competition, and deregulation
Democrats were the party of inclusion, emphasizing redistribution, public subsidies, and social insurance
Republicans argued that big welfare states lead to stagnation and torpor
Democrats countered that unfettered capitalism leads to concentration of wealth and exploitation
Then along came Donald Trump, who disagreed with both of those frameworks
He offered a worldview based on protection, claiming that tariffs and immigration barriers would produce a revival of manufacturing

But Trump’s economic formula has manifestly failed—there are scarcely more manufacturing jobs now than when he first glided down the golden escalator. [ Teresa Ghilarducci: The welfare state: A terrible name for an essential system ] America no longer has a party that offers a full-throated case for economic growth
Instead, the Republican Party resembles an intellectual black hole as it approaches the post-Trump era

The Democratic Party, meanwhile, is being pulled leftward by a bunch of young socialists who champion tried-and-failed policies such as rent control, putting me in mind of that old Richard Weaver maxim: The problem with the younger generation is that they haven’t read the minutes to the last meeting
Here’s why I think the Scandinavians offer us a road map out of this morass: They’re less likely to have our mental categories in their heads
They don’t assume that inclusion and dynamism are at war with each other
They don’t believe you have to choose between capitalism and welfare

Scandinavians have the kind of big supportive welfare systems that make lefties pant in admiration, but most Scandinavians see no contradiction between these systems and aggressive free-market policies
Every year, the libertarian Cato Institute ranks nations in its Human Freedom Index
The Cato ranking system rewards nations for their rule of law, low regulations, free trade, smallish government, property rights, and freedom of religion and expression
In the Cato freedom index, Denmark, Finland, and Sweden all rank higher than the United States
Some people think of the Scandinavian nations as progressive nirvanas
For example, the Swedish economist Andreas Bergh divides his country’s economic history into a series of eras
First came the period of 1870 to 1970, when Sweden rose from abject poverty and became one of the richest nations in Europe
There were a lot of causes for this ascent, but my favorite is the Bildung educational policies that the Swedes adopted in the 19th century
They understood that if their kids were going to contribute to an industrial economy, they would need complex inner lives
They would need to understand complex systems

title: The Download: Better bionic hands and AI’s natural-gas boom
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager
Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics
But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure
For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one’s hand
Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he’s the first to take it home and use it independently
Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system

Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel . —Jessica Hamzelou How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom — Casey Crownhart In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas
Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s been proven right
Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10
Meanwhile, Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s

title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
excerpt: A bionic hand that can feel: Avi Davidson, a 33-year-old trauma therapist who lost his hand at 16, is the first person to take home and independently use an exp
body: A bionic hand that can feel: Avi Davidson, a 33-year-old trauma therapist who lost his hand at 16, is the first person to take home and independently use an experimental prosthetic wired directly to his nerves—letting him feel pressure well enough to crack an egg and make an omelet

Surgery involving a nail gun for nerves: Connecting the device required firing 100-needle electrode arrays into Davidson's arm nerves using a compressed-air gun, since nerves are too floppy for conventional implantation
Phantom wrist strain in a hand with no tendons: Davidson experiences what feels like wrist stiffness in his bionic arm—and relieves it by stretching the prosthetic fingers
Researchers admit this "makes no sense physiologically" and suspect it reflects how the hand is still mapped in his brain

Helping others, not himself: Davidson won't keep the device forever and isn't compensated. "I wanted to help push the technology forward," he says, knowing someone else will eventually benefit more than he does " data-chronoton-post-id="1149923" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager
Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics
But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure
For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand
Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm
But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off
The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year
The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system
The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying
Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life
They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail
They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system
The loss of a limb In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls
But he lost his footing as he tried to descend
He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed
He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too
But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.” Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body
The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up
It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says
The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example
Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says
He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says

New connections A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body
Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one
Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab
Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations

Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one
They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.” In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery

It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George
The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one
Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George
Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says

title: You’ve lived in a red state all your life. Is it wrong to pick up and move to a blue state now?
excerpt: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas
body: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form
Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity: I’m considering moving my family from a red state to a blue state
I’ve lived in a red state my whole life, and as a lesbian with a wonderful trans wife, it is hard
Moving to a blue state could give my wife and I better nondiscrimination protections, better worker protections, and better access to health care
However, I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state
I am well aware of how the red state exodus and the red state brain drain are already affecting our community
It’s hard to weigh what may be best for my wife against what’s best for our fellow red state residents
Dear Should I Stay or Should I Go, I feel your question deep in my bones
Not long ago, I made the decision to move with my partner from the US to Canada, where I’m originally from
And we grappled with many of the same questions you’re wrestling with now

Is it selfish to leave? If you leave, would you be putting your own family’s well-being above the well-being of your wider community? Does that mean you’re reneging on your values?  A few key philosophical ideas really helped me navigate these questions, so I’ll walk you through them
Whether you agree or disagree, they should clarify the terms in a way that makes it easier for you to decide one way or another
Let’s start with your concern about how to weigh what’s best for your wife against what’s best for your wider community

One strain of thought in modern philosophy — promoted by utilitarians like Peter Singer — says that we should aim to maximize the overall good, and that means doing good impartially rather than prioritizing certain people just because they happen to be our nearest and dearest
This perspective has become so influential in the past century that it’s probably shaping your thinking here, even if you’re not explicitly aware of it

Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! But I want you to know that other philosophers have pushed back
Bernard Williams, a staunch critic of utilitarianism, argued that it can actually be totally normal and morally appropriate to show partiality toward our loved ones

In a famous passage, Williams said that if a man sees two people drowning, and one is his wife and the other is a stranger, and he pauses to consider whether rescuing his wife would maximize the overall good more than rescuing the stranger, he has had “ one thought too many .” Williams argued that moral agency does not sit in a contextless vacuum — it is always some specific person’s agency, and as specific people we have specific commitments
When you got together with your wife, you made a commitment to ensuring her well-being, over and above your general wish for all people everywhere to be well
Utilitarianism says you have to consider everyone’s well-being equally, with no special treatment for your own family members — but to Williams, that’s just an absurd demand
It alienates you from a core part of yourself, destroying your integrity as a moral agent
According to this view, putting your wife’s safety first isn’t some moral lapse that should embarrass you
Honoring special obligations to our nearest and dearest is actually part of what makes a life ethical

Besides, even though living an ethical life does sometimes involve being willing to sacrifice some of our own well-being, it’s important to recognize that everybody exists at a different vulnerability level

We shouldn’t expect someone who’s trans to take on risk to the same degree as someone who is not particularly marginalized or endangered.  Given the assault on trans rights in recent years, I’d be really skeptical of anyone who tries to argue that you and your wife have a moral obligation to stay put and “fight the good fight” if she’d be happier and safer elsewhere
Mind you, I also want to caution you to consider all the factors that go into making a happy life before you come to any decision about moving

If your wife has a robust and loving community of friends in your current red state, but knows nobody in the blue state you’re thinking of moving to, she may end up unhappier there on balance. (Plus, as the recent midterms showed, red states don’t necessarily stay red , and even blue states can pass anti-trans rights ballot measures .) I also think a bigger reframe is in order here

You say, “I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state.” But would it really? I’d argue that the key consideration is: Where can you keep fighting the longest? The hardest? The most effectively? The work of contemporary philosopher Lisa Tessman is instructive here

In her book Burdened Virtues , she argues that situations of oppression can demand certain traits of people — like sustained anger at injustice, fierce loyalty to one’s group, constant vigilance and sensitivity to others’ suffering — that can damage the people who embody them even though they are real virtues
These traits can undermine the well-being of the bearers over time, keeping them from flourishing

What’s more, they can potentially even warp their bearers’ moral character — for example, when anger grows into an all-consuming state.  You said that you’ve lived in a red state your whole life and found it hard

So I think it’s worth asking yourself: Are the traits you’ve had to develop under those circumstances — however virtuous they may be — actually eroding your ability to keep showing up, both for yourself and for your wider community, in the way you’d like? If you feel that, say, constant vigilance is starting to take its toll, moving might give you a mental reset that allows you to be more — not less — active in enacting your values

Plus, a quick look at the historical record can defuse the idea that leaving a place means “abandoning the good fight.” Consider what happened in the Great Migration, the exodus of Black Americans from the Jim Crow South
Did those migrants “abandon the good fight”? Absolutely not

Once in the North and West, they built up political power and institutions that ended up feeding into and supporting the civil rights movement .  The point is not that the two situations are exact parallels — they aren’t
The point is that when people leave a place, they can choose to use the affordances of their new home in a way that helps their old home

So, although worries about a red state exodus and red state brain drain are totally understandable, I don’t think they decide the question of whether a move would be net-negative or net-positive for your wider community.  What will decide that is what you choose to do with your newfound resources — including, plausibly, an increased sense of safety, security, and mental health — if you do relocate.  Life gets busy really fast, especially after a big move. (I should know — months after moving, I still haven’t gotten around to putting up any art on my walls!) So, if you leave your home state, my strong recommendation to you is this: Make a plan, in advance, for how you will keep fighting the good fight once you reach your new destination

title: How America broke the turkey
excerpt: Inside a farm that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the second largest US turkey producer. | Photo courtesy of Kecia Doolittle Editor’s note, :  This story was
body: Inside a farm that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the second largest US turkey producer. | Photo courtesy of Kecia Doolittle Editor’s note, :  This story was originally published on November 22, 2023, and reflects events that took place that year
We’re republishing it in its original form for this year’s Thanksgiving week
Late into the night on November 2, 2023, a few animal rights activists opened an unlocked barn door and stepped foot into a sea of turkeys living in gruesome conditions

It was one of several barns at a sprawling factory farming operation in Owatonna, Minnesota, that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the country’s second-largest turkey producer and this year’s supplier to the annual White House turkey pardon ceremony.  Inside this story An undercover investigation into one of America’s biggest turkey companies revealed sick birds in inhumane conditions
Part of the problem is the farms themselves, where turkeys are overcrowded and suffer from high rates of disease
But the biggest problem is the bird’s biology
To boost profits, turkey companies have bred turkeys to grow twice as fast, and nearly twice as big, as they were in the 1960s

The rapid growth causes a range of health issues, and many turkeys are so top-heavy they can hardly walk. “We documented a lot of really horrific health issues,” activist Kecia Doolittle, one of the investigators, told Vox. “It was about as bad as you can imagine.”  They found numerous turkeys who were dead and rotting, Doolittle said, and many who had trouble walking
There were also live birds pecking at dead birds, and dozens of birds with visible wounds — each a sign of cannibalism , a persistent problem in turkey farming
Doolittle also alleges there were a number of turkeys who were immobilized and unable to access food and water

In a letter to Steele County’s attorney and local law enforcement, Bonnie Klapper — a former assistant US attorney advising Doolittle — said the conditions are a violation of Minnesota’s animal cruelty law , which stipulates that “No person shall deprive any animal over which the person has charge or control of necessary food, water, or shelter.” (Minnesota is one of the few states that don’t exempt agricultural practices from their animal cruelty statute.)   “It smelled terrible,” Doolittle said

The air made her throat burn, likely due to high ammonia levels from the turkeys’ waste, which gives the birds eye and respiratory issues .  The activists found a sign on the property that read, “Jennie-O Turkey Store cares about turkeys — you should, too!” “Jennie-O Turkey Store takes the welfare of the animals under our care seriously and has robust animal care standards throughout our supply chain,” a spokesperson from Hormel Foods, Jennie-O’s parent company, told Vox via email. “We conduct routine audits at our facilities to ensure that our standards are being met with animal-handling practices and policies set forth by the National Turkey Federation and the American Veterinary Medical Association.” Doolittle rescued two of the birds — whom she later named Gabriel and Gilbert — and took them to veterinarians in Wisconsin, who urged her to euthanize Gilbert. “They both had really severe infections, they both had parasites,” Doolittle said, but Gilbert was in especially bad shape, with a wound under his wing, an infection on his face, and pecking wounds on part of his genitalia.  But Doolittle wanted to give him a chance to recover

Both birds were treated and given a combination of antibiotic, pain relief, and antiparasitic drugs; Gabriel is on the mend, while Gilbert’s condition remains touch and go.  Sherstin Rosenberg, a veterinarian in California and executive director of a sanctuary for rescued poultry birds , wrote in a veterinary opinion that Gabriel and Gilbert’s condition “suggests serious animal welfare problems” in Jennie-O’s facility
The findings, while disturbing, are common across the turkey industry
Numerous animal welfare groups have found similar conditions at operations run by Jennie-O’s competitors — even the ones that brand themselves as more humane

That’s because turkey farming is incredibly uniform, with companies using generally the same practices and the same breed — the Broad Breasted White turkey — that’s been bred without regard for their suffering

How the poultry industry broke the turkey Like everything else in the US — cars , homes , cruise ships — the turkey has become supersized.  The poultry industry has made turkeys so big primarily through selective breeding
The Broad Breasted White turkey, which accounts for 99 out of every 100 grocery store turkeys , has been bred to emphasize — you guessed it — the breast, one of the more valuable parts of the bird
These birds grow twice as fast and become nearly twice as big as they did in the 1960s
Being so top-heavy, combined with other health issues caused by rapid growth and the unsanitary factory farming environment, can make it difficult for them to walk
Another problem arises from their giant breasts: The males get so big that they can’t mount the hens, so they must be bred artificially
Author Jim Mason detailed this practice in his book The Ethics of What We Eat , co-authored with philosopher Peter Singer

Mason took a job with the turkey giant Butterball to research the book, where, he wrote , he had to hold male turkeys while another worker stimulated them to extract their semen into a syringe using a vacuum pump
Once the syringe was full, it was taken to the henhouse, where Mason would pin hens chest-down while another worker inserted the contents of the syringe into the hen using an air compressor
Workers at the farm had to do this to one hen every 12 seconds for 10 hours a day
It was “the hardest, fastest, dirtiest, most disgusting, worst-paid work” he had ever done, Mason wrote
In stressful, crowded environments, turkeys can be aggressive and peck one another, and even commit cannibalism
Instead of giving turkeys more space and better conditions, producers mutilate them to minimize the damage
They cut off a quarter to a third of their beaks, part of their toes , and their snoods — those fleshy protuberances that hang over their beaks — all without pain relief

Turkeys are excluded from federal laws meant to reduce animal suffering during transport to the slaughterhouse and during slaughter itself, so you can imagine — or see for yourself — how terribly they’re treated in their final hours

According to the nonprofit Animal Welfare Institute, the Jennie-O slaughter plant near the farm Doolittle investigated was cited nine times in 2018 by the US Department of Agriculture for turkeys who’d been mutilated by malfunctioning equipment
Strangely, despite the horrific reality of turkey farming, we still use the animal as a symbol of giving thanks

Nowhere does the song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them feel more disconcerting than at the White House’s annual turkey pardon.  The mixed message of the White House turkey pardon Every Thanksgiving, the US president “pardons” a turkey or two in what is essentially a PR stunt for the turkey industry, as the birds are selected by the chair of the National Turkey Federation, an industry trade association
This year, that was Steve Lykken, president of Jennie-O
The two turkeys selected for this year’s pardon — named Liberty and Bell — could have ended up among the 46 million or so birds on Thanksgiving tables this year

Instead, they were transported from Minnesota, the country’s top turkey-producing state, to Washington, DC, in a stretch black Cadillac Escalade. “They’re on their way in a pretty lavish coach,” Lykken told Minnesota Public Radio

The annual story makes for feel-good if hammy coverage by the nation’s largest news organizations, but it papers over the darkness of American factory farming — including not just the animal cruelty but also the dangerous working conditions at slaughterhouses, environmental pollution , and unfair treatment of turkey contract farmers
The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the Jennie-O investigation video
This year, industry is especially looking forward to the pardon amid the devastating bird flu
The disease, which has been resurging this fall, has resulted in the killing of 11.5 million potentially infected turkeys since early 2022

title: With Melania , We See Nothing
excerpt: “Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania , th
body: “Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania , the movie , or Melania , the memoir , or $Melania , the cryptocurrency )

Melania—typing her name this many times in a row has given me a dizzying feeling of semantic satiation—is sitting on Air Force One, shot in tight focus, wearing a black jacket and a faint scowl. “Of course you think about it,” she replies, revealing teeth so white, they’re almost blue. “You just want to make sure that, you know, the family or my child are taken care of
It’s very in, um, it’s in the stars.” And with that, the question is dismissed, the specter of mortality diffused as rapidly as air from a popped balloon

I can’t say I felt for Ratner, exactly, watching all one hour and 11 minutes of Melania: The Series , because if it weren’t for the allegations of sexual harassment and assault made against him in 2017 (allegations that he denies), he wouldn’t have been exiled to creative Siberia and I wouldn’t have spent multiple hours watching Melania (the Trump) gliding purposefully into the spa at Mar-a-Lago or describing the many exciting benefits that blockchain provides for her fan base

But I’ve spent enough time interviewing resistant subjects to recognize the desperation kicking in as he realizes he’s got nothing . “Have you ever slept in?” he asks at one point. (Not really.) “Do you ever take long walks?” (She doesn’t.) “Do you have a favorite book?” (It’s Melania , of course.) All the while, the camera stays trained on his subject, her eyebrows penciled heavily in two straight lines as if to minimize any human expression she might otherwise convey

Much has been made of how stultifying Melania: The Series is as a televisual experience—how devoid of action! How recycled of content! How toadying in approach! But the series’ emptiness also feels illuminating, in a metatextual kind of way
Ratner gives us such relentless footage of Melania, posed and composed and airtight, that he brings the whole project of documentary filmmaking into disarray

What does it mean to watch someone for such prolonged periods of time and see nothing at all? Every day, we are awash in images and clips—“We sleep and eat the image and pray to it and wear it too,” as Don DeLillo wrote in Mao II . (As if to offer proof, in one scene in Melania: The Series , an assistant director clambers out from behind the camera to show Melania a photo of everything his brother rescued from his house in Los Angeles before it burned down in the 2025 wildfires—his guitars and his MAGA hats.) The president is a booster of artificially generated imagery, which tends to suit his particular aesthetic: gaudy, emotionally staged, ideological

And the most dominant movie of the moment is a documentary, You Can See Everything , which, like Melania , manipulates the visual and aural language of film, but as anti-propaganda, to show us how profoundly untrustworthy it has been all along
In that nearly three-hour movie, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, Elizabeth Holmes’s face, like Melania’s, absorbs the camera
Fielder moves in with the disgraced Theranos founder and her partner, Billy Evans, in the weeks before she goes to prison for fraud
Holmes seems to be under the impression that through what Evans calls “radical transparency” she can persuade Fielder, and the rest of us, of her innocence

And so, for a few weeks, a pair of the most practiced illusionists in American culture go head-to-head in her rented, wood-paneled beach house: the Silicon Valley saleswoman and the comedian so committed to the bit that he once trained for almost two and a half years to become a commercial pilot, in service of his TV show
Two manipulators, each alike in proficiency
The question seems to be less about which one will prevail—Fielder has the lopsided power of final cut—than about whether anything unexpected will be revealed in the process

From the beginning, Fielder and Oppenheim use angles and lighting to set up stock roles: Holmes, the mother clutching an infant, awash in natural light, is the heroine; Fielder, lurking in the darkness and grimacing, is her antagonist
Her face is almost ludicrously likable on camera, rubberized and wide-eyed, guileless, and the movie zooms in on it well past the point of discomfort
Holmes weeps, she breaks down, she locks eyes with Fielder so intently that the pair seem to be glued to each other

All this looking gives Fielder no insight into what to make of her, so in the second half of the film, after she goes to jail, he restages scenes of their meetings and even seeks the help of a professional actor to try to get inside her head

Holmes remains unknowable, much as Melania does, despite all the time we’ve spent watching her , despite the “equivocal magic” of the image, as Susan Sontag once wrote, and despite the fact that You Can See Everything uses scenes and images to provoke every emotional response in the handbook: shock (unexpected full-frontal nudity), pathos (a devastated Holmes being led into prison), suspense (Hitchcockian angles and shadows)
The score, by Ari Balouzian, all jagged strings and low, discordant humming, similarly seems intent on trying to make us feel
For all of its prolonged run time, the movie is riveting
But it also clearly lays its tricks on the table: Storytelling is a fundamentally manipulative process, Fielder seems to argue by the end
Ratner uses many of the same techniques as Fielder to elicit emotion in Melania —heavy-handed aural hooks, close-ups, shameless scenes of devastation
He comes up short, but perhaps that’s because he lacks the true skill of canny scammers and filmmakers: sensing what people, in all our glorious and idiotic humanity, really want to see.

title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
excerpt: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, including fr
body: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, including from data centers
Nearly half the capacity of new proposals in the country's largest grid came from gas plants

Big tech's emissions are climbing fast: Meta's greenhouse-gas emissions jumped 45% in a single year — outpacing Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — and the company is quietly reconsidering its 2030 net-zero commitment

Companies are building their own power plants: Unable to wait for grid connections, data center developers have proposed over 100 off-grid gas facilities since early 2025, with combined capacity more than double California's peak electricity demand. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149836" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas
Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right
Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries
But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence
Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too
The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10
And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants
How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system
In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today
But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC
PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals
In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue
Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue
PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US

Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.  This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies
Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report
That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% )
The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead
It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power
Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well)
Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source
But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers
Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California)
The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025
There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example
I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
AI is straining America’s open records systems AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records

Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments
At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests
As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests
That could potentially make public offices less transparent

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know . —Matthew King MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below
Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground
Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases
Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle
But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking? This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts

title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
excerpt: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all
body: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all
He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer
During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests
Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper
Last year, those requests started coming quarterly
Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares

These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”  Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US
While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest

Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments
At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests
Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years

While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.  As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.  Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law
Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools

But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.  This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days

Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration
What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says
SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data
Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies
The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer

Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks
The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”  While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data

For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada
That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites
NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment
The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI
But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices
In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job

Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell
In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says
A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used
FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day , she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year
The AI detection problem It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests

Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection

David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025

The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.  In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests
Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula

But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.  While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests
Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance
Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages

title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
