<title>Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773171/original/file-20261119-62-t0qpui.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2052%2C0%2C2888%2C1925&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Monks Mound towers over the land at the Cahokia archaeological complex in Illinois.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monk%27s_mound_panorama.jpg">TimVickers via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was <a href="https://www.isas.illinois.edu/research_2/cahokia">once home to 20,000 people</a> near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.</p>

<p>My anthropology colleague <a href="https://www.anthropology.wisc.edu/staff/schroeder-sissel/">Sissel Schroeder</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=k4JPb8wAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">I</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">studied both sites</a> to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.  </p>



<h2>Archaeological sites forming in a modern community</h2>

<p>During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/history-of-the-centreville-sewage-crisis">mismanaged drainage infrastructure</a>. Yet in <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/interviews">interviews with a community group, residents reported</a> that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came. </p>

<p><iframe id="geFJ9" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/geFJ9/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Three line charts that show total precipitation, average temperature and population numbers."></iframe></p>

<p>From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by <a href="https://www.weather.gov/media/lsx/climate/stl/precip/precip_stl_ranked_annual_amounts.pdf">10 inches</a> (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more <a href="https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/walter-johnson-detroit-tk/">frequent flooding</a>, including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/">back up raw sewage</a> into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.</p>

<p>Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, <a href="https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/illinois/a-plea-for-help-centreville-s-sewage-and-drainage-problems-pose-health-safety-risks/article_3d6d22c7-8c57-5d1a-8af3-a6e6ee6ea2ee.html">leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes</a>. Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of photos show buildings in varying degrees of disrepair." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Street-view photos of Centreville show abandoned (A, B) and demolished (C) houses, structure foundations (D,E) and a school building (F,G) that has since been demolished.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">White and Schroeder, 2026.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>An ancient city</h2>

<p>Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound. </p>

<p><a href="https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-38-monks-mound/">Monks Mound</a> is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SpccDCKeQts">chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears</a> – <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/woodhenge-cahokia">timber monuments</a> likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing <a href="https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-72/">elaborate burials</a>.</p>

<p><iframe id="3qQkc" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3qQkc/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map showing the relative locations of Centreville, Cahokia and St. Louis."></iframe></p>

<p>Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2018.03.009">continued for 200 years</a>. Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/285045502_Contemplating_Cahokia's_Collapse">range of societal and environmental theories</a>.</p>

<h2>Climate change at Cahokia</h2>

<p>In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1809400116">Cahokia experienced several natural disasters</a> during a warming period known as the <a href="https://theconversation.com/climate-explained-what-was-the-medieval-warm-period-155294">Medieval Climatic Anomaly</a>. In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1809400116">those climatic changes</a>.</p>

<p>Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like <a href="https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/before-and-after-the-day-after-tomorrow/">catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow</a>.” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.</p>

<p>As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694566">archaeological evidence</a> suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">Larger houses and status symbols</a> became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A diagram of the landscape and human-occupied areas of Cahokia." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=463&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=463&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=463&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=582&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=582&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773152/original/file-20261119-62-4p45nl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=582&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Central Cahokia was at the edge of the Mississippi River’s lower floodplain.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">White and Schroeder, 2026.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The past and future of climate change</h2>

<p>To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.  </p>

<p>People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “<a href="https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/illinois/a-plea-for-help-centreville-s-sewage-and-drainage-problems-pose-health-safety-risks/article_3d6d22c7-8c57-5d1a-8af3-a6e6ee6ea2ee.html">I’m not going to abandon my house</a>. It’s all I got.” </p>

<p>Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.</p>

<p>At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">most exposed to crop loss from flooding</a>, but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.</p>

<p>People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to <a href="https://doi.org/10.5876/9781607323808.c009">communal feasts</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">shared food storage</a>. I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society. </p>

<p>If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">some benefited, some lost</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2018.03.009">some left</a>.</p>

<p>Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as <a href="https://theconversation.com/nepals-flash-floods-show-the-devastating-power-of-cascading-hazards-290611">sudden massive floods</a>. But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.</p>

<p>Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.</p>

<p>Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294435/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure
At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways
Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding , but plots in the uplands were safer
During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils
People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage
I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave
Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society

Shown here is her work &#39;Violet Obsession.&#39;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/violet-obsession-part-of-yayoi-kusama-infinite-mirrors-news-photo/647003398">Bill O&#39;Leary/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Japanese artist <a href="https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/yayoi-kusama-8094/introduction-yayoi-kusama">Yayoi Kusama’s</a> installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the <a href="https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/p/pop-art">pop art</a> scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the <a href="https://theconversation.com/before-the-infinity-nets-there-was-the-pacific-ocean-what-origin-stories-focusing-on-yayoi-kusamas-mental-illness-miss-about-her-art-290760">source of her creativity</a>. Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications. </p>

<p>Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world? </p>

<p>Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created <a href="https://www.moma.org/audio/playlist/297/4027">Accumulation No. 1</a>, her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical <a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/infinity-rooms/">Infinity Mirror Rooms</a> installation.</p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/works-by-yayoi-kusama-on-display-at-the-yayoi-kusama-news-photo/148196135">J. Countess/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A major retrospective of her work is <a href="https://www.stedelijk.nl/nl/tentoonstellingen/yayoi-kusama">on view at the Stedelijk Museum</a> through Jan. 17, 2027.</p>

<p>The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zFzYmJwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">art historian</a> who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.</p>

<h2>Phallic focus</h2>

<p>Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the <a href="https://www.moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/3663">male-dominated New York art world</a>. During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants. </p>

<p>Painter <a href="https://www.moma.org/collection/works/78375">Grace Hartigan</a> had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor <a href="https://buffaloakg.org/person/marisol">Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition</a> at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.</p>

<p>Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond <a href="https://www.britannica.com/art/Abstract-Expressionism">abstract expressionism</a>. The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/778410">coded as masculine</a>. Pop artists <a href="https://www.guggenheim-bilbao.eus/en/exhibition/gallery-303-echoes-of-pop-art">refused this model</a>: They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production. </p>

<p>Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became <a href="https://www.moma.org/interactives/exhibitions/1998/kusama/manual/kusama_10.html">Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show</a>. She decided to focus on sewing — an art <a href="https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1390572174767769472">rooted in her female Japanese education</a> — and she ordered a sewing machine.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="White boat covered in white protrusions, set in a room patterned with the same image" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Yayoi Kusama’s Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show (1963) was shown in a retrospective of her work at Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam in 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-photograph-shows-the-artwork-aggregation-one-thousand-news-photo/2293764340">Lina Selg / AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a <a href="https://dictionary.apa.org/phallocentric">symbol of patriarchal authority</a> – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft. </p>

<p>In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.</p>

<h2>Neurosis or intention?</h2>

<p>Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as <a href="https://www.artsy.net/article/editorial-kusamas-infinity-nets-channel-the-creative-power">evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis</a>. But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.</p>

<p>In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1893269/">sew the protrusions</a> on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.</p>

<p>Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while <a href="https://yayoikusamastore.com/en/products/e-bojp01a6">she was exploring “kyōfu”</a> – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for <a href="https://dn790003.ca.archive.org/0/items/freud-uncanny_001/freud-uncanny_001_text.pdf">the uncanny</a> is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called <a href="https://theconversation.com/penis-envy-the-oedipus-complex-and-authentic-paths-to-meaning-25-writers-from-siri-hustvedt-to-colm-toibin-reflect-on-freuds-legacy-240684">penis envy</a>.  </p>

<h2>Male authority</h2>

<p>Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/779235">satire of penis envy</a>. And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power. </p>

<p>In one of her <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/39030076">self-portraits from 1966</a>, Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist <a href="https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/louise-bourgeois-2351/art-louise-bourgeois">Louise Bourgeois</a>, who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including <a href="https://www.moma.org/collection/works/81418">Fillette (Little Girl)</a>, that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.</p>

<p>But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1962/06/17/archives/seasons-end-abstractions-and-distractions-gigantism-way-out.html">gave her work only a brief mention</a>. When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he <a href="https://archive.org/details/sim_arts-magazine_1962-11_37_2">received rave reviews</a> in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.</p>



<p>Kusama’s popularity today stems from works that are both visually expansive and socially subversive. <a href="https://play.qagoma.qld.gov.au/looknowseeforever/timeline/">Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show</a> was her first all-over exhibit – an exhibition in which a repeated motif covers the gallery’s four walls, drawing the audience into the work rather than asking them to view it as a separate object. On display at the Gertrude Stein Gallery from December 1963 to January 1964, it featured a sculpture of the phallus-embedded boat surrounded by its image repeating across the wall. </p>

<p>Although Kusama sought to subvert male authority, she appears nude in a <a href="https://play.qagoma.qld.gov.au/looknowseeforever/timeline/">photograph of the phallus boat installation</a>, her back to the camera, trapped between the real and the illusory. Rowing the boat seems like the only way to escape the omnipresence of masculinity. </p>

<p>She seemed even more entrapped by patriarchal symbolism in her Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli’s Field, where she lays among an array of phalluses covered in red polka dots.</p>

<h2>Psychedelic culture</h2>

<p>In 1966, Kusama found a way to break away from male domination through her “<a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/the-exhibition/">Peep Show</a>” at the Castellane Gallery in New York. In it, she reduced the towering phallus to a small dot of light. It was her first work of <a href="https://artincontext.org/psychedelic-art/">psychedelic art</a>, a category the curator Christoph Grunenberg characterized as both “<a href="https://thecarycollection.com/products/summer-of-love-art-of-the-psychedelic-era-2007-grunenberg-christoph-edited-by">artistic experiment and dissenting politics</a>.”</p>

<p>Incorporating Beatles music, flickering strobe lights and mirror reflections, “Peep Show” was intended to produce effects similar to those of psychoactive drugs such as mescaline, psilocybin and LSD, liberating users from established social norms and opening the possibility of alternative values. The exhibit, later known as “<a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/the-exhibition/">Love Forever</a>,” also aimed to alter perception by <a href="https://theconversation.com/curious-kids-why-do-people-with-synaesthesia-link-senses-and-how-does-it-work-160565">inducing synesthesia</a> — a neurological state in which stimulating one sensory-cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ahZh_Qpb8ik?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms continue to dazzle crowds.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://library.cca.edu/bib/26390">Kusama remembered</a> attending a lecture by <a href="https://psychology.fas.harvard.edu/people/timothy-leary">Timothy Leary</a>, a former Harvard University psychology professor and psychedelics advocate, at the Village Theater in New York, a hub of psychedelic culture. In 1968, she collaborated with light artist Joshua White on <a href="https://live-thebroadmuseum.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/pressroom/2017.10.11_kusama_infinity_mirrors_programming_release_final.pdf">Self-Obliteration</a>, a fusion of sound, lights and images that Leary claimed “would demonstrate what an LSD session is like.” </p>

<p>Kusama’s ability to transform any neurosis she may have had into liberation began with Accumulation No. 1 and continued through <a href="https://whitney.org/collection/works/19436">Fireflies on the Water</a> (2002), <a href="https://collection.qagoma.qld.gov.au/objects/14351">Soul Under the Moon</a> (2002), <a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/infinity-rooms#aftermath">Infinity Mirror Room—Aftermath of Obliteration of Eternity</a> (2009) and <a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/infinity-rooms#souls">Infinity Mirrored Room—The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away</a> (2013). The ethereal visions embodied in her psychedelic mirror rooms <a href="https://academicworks.cuny.edu/gc_etds/4328/">stand in for the mind-altering drugs</a> that release people from the rationality of society and fuel the desire to change.</p>

<p>Through Kusama’s Accumulation and Infinity Mirror Room series, I argue that she turned the human body into what philosopher Herbert Marcuse described as “<a href="https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/marcuse/works/eros-civilisation/preface.htm">an instrument of pleasure</a>.” By making the body an instrument of pleasure rather than labor, Kusama subverted the age-old patriarchal order.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290804/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Georgians mark 2 years of pro-EU demonstrations – defying campaign to wear protesters down</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773818/original/file-20261124-62-47lvsv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Demonstrators with Georgian and European Union flags fly in the capital of Tbilisi on Nov. 28, 2025, to mark what was then a year of nonstop protests against the government. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Europe%20Georgia%20Visas/6d68f201f9a042268f9521863ea8a236/photo">AP Photo/Zurab Tsertsvadze</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For months on end, Georgians have braved the elements and long odds to protest their government’s suspension of the former Soviet country’s bid to join the European Union. On Nov. 28, 2026, those pro-democracy campaigners will mark a milestone – two years of sustained, if declining, protest.</p>

<p>Hailed as a beacon of democracy following its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Georgia has of late been increasingly held up as <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/dangers-democratic-backsliding-georgia">an example</a> of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/jod.2016.0012">democratic backsliding</a>: the slow, persistent erosion of democratic institutions. Indeed, the 2025 <a href="https://www.eiu.com/n/campaigns/democracy-index-2025/">Economist Democracy Index</a> — an annual benchmark of global democratic health — found that Georgia had fallen 20 places on the list since 2017.</p>

<p>The formal hallmarks of democratic systems remain visible: Elections are held, parliaments vote and political parties organize. At the same time, <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/03/13/new-osce-report-finds-sharp-democratic-backsliding-in-georgia">democratic institutions are compromised</a> by political leaders, parties, police, courts and legislators – who use their resources to <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/06/georgia-authorities-built-coordinated-system-to-crush-dissent-and-entrench-power/">stifle dissent</a> and <a href="https://scholarlycommons.law.emory.edu/elj/vol73/iss5/4/">compromise democratic institutions</a> .</p>

<p>These leaders commonly target electoral fairness without committing blatant fraud. For example, <a href="https://eu.boell.org/en/2024/10/29/2024-elections-georgia-descent-hegemonic-authoritarianism">public sector workers</a> such as teachers are threatened with job loss if they do not vote for the government, or <a href="https://transparency.ge/en/post/misuse-administrative-resources-parliamentary-elections-2024-interim-report">local governments</a> are rewarded for producing votes during elections. Critics allege that <a href="https://www.amnestyusa.org/reports/anatomy-of-repression-georgia-500-days-of-protest-crackdown-and-resilience/">biased laws</a> and politicized court cases <a href="https://ipi.media/georgia-an-escalating-media-freedom-crisis/">eliminate independent media</a> and jail opposition leaders.</p>

<p>Backsliding governments also use <a href="https://susan-stokes.com/books/book-info/backsliders.html">disinformation and rhetoric</a> to create confusion and fear. Using these tactics, critics allege, the ruling populist right, pro-Russian Georgian Dream government continues to undermine the fragile democracy. With many feeling unable to fight back through elections and parliamentary debates, Georgians have taken <a href="https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/articles/the-source-of-georgias-democratic-resilience/">to the streets</a>.</p>

<p>I am a member of a research project <a href="https://reginasmyth.com/research/">that explores</a> how national protests in countries with fragile democratic institutions create legacies that can influence politics over the long term. In Georgia, that work is based on interviews with leaders from across civic and political life. These interviews point to a widespread view that the government is actively attempting to erode protest just as critics of the government feel it has eroded institutions. So far, the government has not crushed the movement with a campaign of lethal force. Rather, it has tried to use lower-level, but sustained, suppression tactics in hopes of inducing <a href="https://afsee.atlanticfellows.lse.ac.uk/en-gb/blogs/unjust-tackling-activist-burnout-in-an-unequal-world-why-it-matters-and-what-we-can-do-about-it">burnout in the opposition</a> and getting civil society to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/socf.70085">disengage</a>.</p>

<h2>The seeds of popular uprising</h2>

<p>In Georgia, the roots of protest are deep in the struggle for independence from the Soviet Union and the influence of Russia under the leadership of Vladimir Putin. In 2003, Georgians launched the <a href="https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/articles/georgias-rose-revolution/">Rose Revolution</a> – the first in a series of actions across the former Soviet states called the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/jod.0.0010">Color Revolutions</a> – to support democracy and autonomy from the Russian Federation. </p>

<p>The Georgian Dream emerged as a socially conservative opposition party in 2012 under the leadership of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili and won a majority of seats in parliamentary elections. Many analysts at the time saw the party as a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/jod.2013.0002">new chance</a> to consolidate democracy. Yet unable to provide <a href="https://jamestown.org/five-years-taking-power-georgian-dreams-promises-remain-unfulfilled/">economic gains</a>, the party instead embarked on a platform consistent with pro-Russian security policies, which critics allege were rife with <a href="https://gip.ge/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Policy-Memo-76-1.pdf">political manipulation, and false rhetoric</a> that undermined democracy. In <a href="https://www.rferl.org/a/thousands-stage-anti-government-protest-in-tbilisi/30175687.html">2019</a>, Georgians took to the streets to contest <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/11/15/protests-erupt-georgia-over-failed-electoral-reforms">failed electoral reforms</a> and growing Russian influence through Ivanishvili’s governance.</p>

<p>By 2023, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-64893359">tens of thousands</a> of Georgians filled Rustaveli Avenue in the capital of Tbilisi to oppose a law designed to shutter civic organizations and independent media. The so-called <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/dangers-democratic-backsliding-georgia">Russia Law</a> borrowed heavily from the Kremlin’s tactics to eliminate opposition to the Putin government in Russia. Many Georgians understood the law as an attack on democracy and celebrated when the ruling party, Georgian Dream, <a href="https://www.politico.eu/article/georgia-tbilisi-government-abandons-russia-putin-style-foreign-agent-bill/">withdrew its bill</a>. </p>

<p>A year later, as new elections approached, the party reintroduced the law, provoking renewed protest. This time it passed. A few months later, <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur56/1115/2026/en/">preelection polls</a> showed the opposition parties leading, but expectations of victory evaporated when Georgia Dream secured 54% of vote – an outcome that critics raised as a possible indicator of <a href="https://css.ethz.ch/content/dam/ethz/special-interest/gess/cis/center-for-securities-studies/pdfs/caucasusanalyticaldigest-141.pdf">electoral manipulation</a>. </p>

<p>Then, on Nov. 28, 2024, the new government put Georgia’s <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2024/11/30/us-suspends-partnership-georgia-00192044">European Union bid on hold</a> until 2028. Many Georgians have long seen EU membership as a path forward to <a href="https://www.thenewfederalist.eu/the-pro-european-attitude-of-georgian-youth-ideals-frustrations-and-the">economic growth</a> and <a href="https://www.vox.com/world-politics/389362/georgia-protests-eu-georgian-dream-russia">democratic protections</a>. In light of Russia’s 2008 occupation of Georgian territory and 2022 full-scale war in Ukraine, Georgians also perceived <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/mar/07/georgia-expedites-eu-application-in-policy-u-turn-russia-ukraine">EU membership</a> as a bulwark against Russian intervention.</p>

<p>Fueled by feelings of betrayal over the reversal on EU membership, crowds <a href="https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/online-exclusive/georgias-battle-for-freedom/">poured back</a> onto Rustaveli Avenue, <a href="https://cepa.org/article/between-east-and-west-georgia-hangs-in-the-balance/">reaching a peak</a> of 170,000-200,000 protesters. Several hundred activists have returned every day since.</p>

<h2>The government’s plan for opposition burnout</h2>

<p>Over the course of two years, Georgian protesters have faced <a href="https://apnews.com/article/georgia-russia-crackdown-protests-european-union-40cef7f965eb796ab23443f1c66d439b">chronic and unpredictable violence</a> rather than a decisive crackdown. By <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur56/1115/2026/en/">Amnesty International’s count</a>, thousands have been arrested, hundreds beaten in the streets or abused in custody, and more than 150 imprisoned after politically motivated trials.</p>

<p>In general, however, the Georgian government’s tactic for countering the protest movement has been to avoid mass violence in lieu of targeted attacks on protest leaders and subtler means to discourage new activists. Fines for protest rose tenfold between 2024 and 2026 to double the average Georgian’s monthly income, leading <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur56/1115/2026/en/">Amnesty International</a> to conclude that Georgia’s courts have become tools for “financially exhausting protesters.” Meanwhile, <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/12/04/georgia-repressive-laws-effectively-criminalize-peaceful-protests">repeat offenses for participating in a demonstration</a> have become crimes.</p>

<p>These actions have steadily increased the costs of protesting, driving activists from the streets due to a multitude of reasons related to risk, personal safety and fear. In our research, we protect the people we interviewed from state retaliation by making them anonymous.</p>

<p>The effects of these costs are clear in their statements.</p>

<p>“We don’t say it openly,” an investigative journalist and editor told us. “But the truth is, we were exhausted, depleted — and that’s the state we were in when the election campaign started.” </p>

<p>Another pro-European student movement member said, “Human resources are exhausted. You can’t expect 300,000 or 100,000 or even 20,000 people to march from Ilia University to Parliament every single day for 200 or 300 days straight. People have jobs, lives, personal struggles, and you can’t ask them to drop everything every day.” </p>

<p>Overall, our interviews with a variety of civil society leaders and protest supporters found that exhaustion was widespread and that a declining amount of people had the physical, financial or emotional capacity to stand every day. </p>

<p>Still, leaders remain hopeful that the nightly protests will provide a platform for renewed activism when the next opportunity for challenging the government presents itself. As the same pro-European student movement member argued: “I believe that will change. Let’s say Georgians are just on a kind of protest vacation. I hope we’ll be back out there again, all together, very soon.”</p>

<p>For now, there exists an effective stalemate between the protest movement and the government. The movement endures but has not broken through, and I believe the government cannot crush it because it fears the student leader is right — and the protest vacation might end. </p>

<h2>The implications beyond Georgia</h2>

<p>For a generation of Georgians invested in building democracy, the past two years have shown how quickly democratic gains can be undone.</p>

<p>Still, as the anniversary of nightly protests approaches, many Georgians point to Serbia, where <a href="https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/online-exclusive/how-serbian-students-created-the-largest-protest-movement-in-decades/">student protesters</a> also took the streets in November 2024 and forced an early election on Oct. 25, 2026. The same Serbian students formed an opposition bloc that won a parliamentary majority that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/world/europe/serbia-student-list-news-media-vucic.html">unseated an entrenched and increasingly autocratic leader</a>. </p>

<p>Georgian Dream understands this threat and has proposed a ban on opposition parties, closing the route that Serbia’s students used.</p>

<p>Yet a policy of attrition has its risk, as ruling in that manner can further erode legitimacy and incur the high costs of keeping elites loyal. In the meantime, the protests continue, which could yet provide oxygen for renewed opposition when a new crisis arises. </p>

<title>Columbia is keeping its gates closed, raising the question of what universities owe their neighborhoods</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773985/original/file-20261124-62-mr10rq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=120%2C61%2C5435%2C3623&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A Columbia University public safety officer locks a campus gate on the first day of fall semester in September 2025 in New York City. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/columbia-university-public-safety-officer-locks-a-campus-news-photo/2232787377?phrase=Columbia%20university%20campus%20closed&amp;adppopup=true">Mostafa Bassim/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The <a href="https://abcnews.com/US/pro-palestinian-protests-unfolded-college-campuses-us-timeline/story?id=109902300">Gaza war protests</a> that overtook <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/05/18/1251915545/pro-palestinian-protests-students-interview-columbia-cuny-hunter-nyc">some colleges</a> and <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/05/07/1249368151/gaza-college-protest-deal-brown-rutgers">universities in 2023 and 2024 have</a> long dispersed – but one very clear remnant of the demonstrations remains at Columbia University’s Morningside Heights campus in New York City: a closed campus.</p>

<p>Columbia’s administration first shut the gates in April 2024, following pro-Palestinian rights protests and <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2024/05/01/new-york-mayor-outside-agitators-columbia-protest-00155581">waves of police arrests</a>. New York City politicians <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/04/nyregion/columbia-protests-arrest-agitators-israel.html">said that these disruptions</a> were fueled by “outside agitators.”</p>

<p>Now, only students, faculty, staff and alumni with a school ID <a href="https://www.columbiaspectator.com/news/2026/11/11/judge-rules-columbia-can-keep-gates-closed/">are able to enter</a> Columbia’s quad.</p>

<p>Some of Columbia’s neighbors <a href="https://iapps.courts.state.ny.us/fbem/DocumentDisplayServlet?documentId=0hqsK_PLUS_Bz6D3ABudOrvXNdg==&amp;system=prod">sued the university</a> in January 2025, <a href="https://iapps.courts.state.ny.us/fbem/DocumentDisplayServlet?documentId=0hqsK_PLUS_Bz6D3ABudOrvXNdg==&amp;system=prod">saying that</a> the closure created a “six-block barrier between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue from West 120th to West 114th Street” and violated the <a href="https://www.ada.gov/resources/disability-rights-guide/">Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act</a>. </p>

<p>A New York Supreme Court judge in Manhattan <a href="https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/28881307/judge-dismisses-philippe-auffray-et-al-v-columbia-university-in-the-city-of-new-york.pdf">dismissed their suit</a> on Nov. 10, 2026, saying that “even if Columbia previously granted unrestricted public access to College Walk, as it remained their private property, nothing prevented them from restricting access at any time.” The plaintiffs quickly <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/nyregion/columbia-college-walk-pathway-public-closure.html">appealed the decision</a>.</p>

<p>Columbia <a href="https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/28881307/judge-dismisses-philippe-auffray-et-al-v-columbia-university-in-the-city-of-new-york.pdf">has maintained that safety concerns meant it needed to close</a> its gates, and that the campus is private property. </p>

<p>Nonetheless, in the past, Columbia allowed neighbors to cross the campus as a scenic shortcut through the neighborhood. Nearby nursery schools used the campus green as a place for children to explore and play.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.amherst.edu/people/facstaff/adsarat">college professor of law</a> and political science, and an <a href="https://www.joneslibrary.org/trustees">elected official in the western Massachusetts town where I teach</a>, the Columbia campus controversy feels familiar. These <a href="https://capturingcambridge.org/explore-by-theme/town-and-gown-the-struggle-and-story-in-cambridge/">“town-and-gown” disputes</a> have, from time to time, raised questions about what universities owe the community beyond their gates. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People walk behind a metal barricade near a NYPD white police van with blue writing." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773997/original/file-20261124-62-586s7m.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People take part in a protest outside Columbia University in 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-take-part-in-a-protest-outside-columbia-university-news-photo/2206743864?phrase=Columbia%20university%20protest&amp;adppopup=true">Kena Betancur/VIEWpress via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Town-and-gown conflicts</h2>

<p>From at least the 1950s until 2024, Columbia had an open campus policy. In 1953, New York City <a href="https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/issue/fall17/article/uniting-columbias-campus">approved closing the campus’s central West 116th Street</a> stretch to cars, with the understanding that pedestrians would be able to walk across the campus. </p>

<p>The recent closure stirred up tensions between the school and its neighbors. But such strains are as old as universities themselves. Some <a href="https://historyofeducation.net/2020/09/02/the-bad-tempered-backstory-of-town-versus-gown/">commentators suggest</a> that conflict between universities and their surrounding communities can be traced back to medieval Europe. </p>

<p>“The early universities in cities such as Bologna and Paris took a very different form to the institutions we know today. They were loose communities of masters and scholars who lived amongst the people of the town,” the education historian <a href="https://historyofeducation.net/2020/09/02/the-bad-tempered-backstory-of-town-versus-gown/">Harley Richardson wrote in 2020</a>. </p>

<p>Townspeople often resented those scholars and students because “They couldn’t understand the scholarly Latin spoken by the students” or whether “the long gowns they wore” were “intended to convey a superior social status,” Richardson wrote.</p>

<p>One of the most notorious town-gown incidents that turned violent <a href="https://www.oxfordhistory.org.uk/mayors/government/scholastica.html">occurred</a> in Oxford, England, in February 1354 on so-called St. Scholastica Day, <a href="https://www.vaticannews.va/en/saints/02/10/st--scolastica--virgin--sister-di-s--benedetto.html">honoring an Italian saint who founded the order of the Benedictine nuns</a>.</p>

<p>Trouble began in a local tavern when some students complained loudly and aggressively about the poor quality of the wine they were served. Things escalated when the tavern-keeper, who was also the mayor of Oxford, responded with insults. A fight broke out and drew in a large number of townspeople and students who rushed to the scene. It took the intervention of the king to restore order. </p>

<p>Conflicts between universities and their local towns or cities <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1933/09/16/that-was-college-life">have also been very much a part</a> of the story of higher education in the United States. </p>

<p>Most often <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/marvinkrislov/2026/11/20/how-universities-help-shape-the-cities-they-call-home/">these disputes have focused</a> on issues like where a university should build a dormitory or whether it should pay fees to the city where it is located. </p>

<p>And as in England, these conflicts have occasionally turned violent. </p>

<p>One such incident happened in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1806, when riots broke out <a href="https://archives.yalealumnimagazine.com/issues/01_03/town_gown.html">between Yale University students</a> and locals who were on their way to church.</p>

<h2>Universities’ civic responsibilities</h2>

<p>What, if anything, <a href="https://podcasts.apple.com/in/podcast/what-do-universities-owe-society-with-ron-daniels/id1642334178?i=1000733876703&amp;l=pa">do universities owe their communities</a>? </p>

<p>The popular phrase “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-022-00341-0">the ivory tower</a>” captures one vision of a university. It suggests that universities serve society by being left alone to conduct research and educate students, disengaged from the larger community’s immediate concerns. In this view, people outside of universities benefit indirectly from the inventions and innovations that universities produce, as well as from the jobs they create. </p>

<p>Another vision, which came to prominence in the 1960s, <a href="https://digitalcommons.unomaha.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1127&amp;context=slcehighered">called on universities to be good citizens</a> of their surrounding communities. This view <a href="https://www.facingsouth.org/2025/08/what-do-universities-owe-communities-interview-davarian-baldwin">urged university leaders</a> to invest in their neighborhoods. </p>

Bukaty/Associated Press</a></span>
            </figcaption>

<p>Colby College, in Waterville, Maine, <a href="https://news.colby.edu/story/a-new-report-measures-colbys-economic-impact/">exemplifies this approach</a>. It has spent US$265 million on construction and other investment projects over the past <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2023/01/16/colby-revitalizes-downtown-waterville">several years</a>, with an eye on revitalizing <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/02/25/business/colleges-downtowns-investment.html">its struggling downtown district</a>. </p>

<p>Others schools, including the <a href="https://stories.nd.edu/stories/rolling-out-the-welcome-mat/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">University of Notre Dame</a>, the <a href="https://almanac.upenn.edu/articles/penn-medicine-invests-3-million-in-south-and-southwest-philadelphia-to-support-storm-recovery-initiative-led-by-deeply-rooted">University of Pennsylvania</a>, the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/15/realestate/commercial/usc-village-los-angeles-campus.html">University of Southern California</a> and the <a href="https://www.ucsf.edu/news/2021/11/421841/ucsf-launches-community-investment-program-support-housing-and-minority-owned">University of California, San Francisco</a>, have invested substantial amounts of money in <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/higher-education-cities-hidden-asset/">developing their towns and cities</a> and supporting neighbors. Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, for example, announced in September 2026 that <a href="https://www.trincoll.edu/news/trinity-college-unveils-major-financial-aid-initiatives/">it would pay for the full tuition</a>, housing and meals for local residents who are admitted as students. </p>

<p>Some universities <a href="https://www.fivecolleges.edu/academics/community-based-learning">have been sending students out into the communities around them</a> as one way to support their city. For example, Columbia Journalism School students <a href="https://journalism.columbia.edu/CJS2030/LocalNonprofitNews">are often tasked</a> with developing a reporting project in a particular New York City neighborhood.</p>

<p>And some leaders in higher education now <a href="https://www.wesleyan.edu/about/news/2026/07/blog/higher-ed-at-americas-250.html">talk openly</a>  about <a href="https://www.amherst.edu/news/news_releases/2023/november/governor-healey-and-president-elliott-talk-democracy">orienting their schools</a> toward the promotion of the greater good.</p>

<h2>Closing gates or building bridges</h2>

<p>A university investing in its surrounding community does not guarantee the end of tensions, which to me seem an inevitable part of the higher education landscape.</p>

<p>But when universities show their communities that civic responsibility is core to their mission, they build goodwill and offer a way of bridging divides when conflicts occur. </p>

<p>I don’t know how the Columbia campus dispute will resolve. But as newly elected New York State Assemblyman <a href="https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/news/2026/11/19/students-neighbors-question-columbia-over-locked-campus-entrances">Eli Northrop observed</a>: “Columbia is successful when Morningside Heights is successful and when the relationship between the neighborhood and the university is good.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297102/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Immersive shopping has survived the demise of the metaverse – but its appeal depends on how it’s designed and who is using it</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/774047/original/file-20261124-62-kdb3pm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5456%2C3637&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Sophie Helen Rhys-Jones, the Duchess of Edinburgh, tries out virtual try-on technology in 2024.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/the-duchess-of-edinburgh-patron-of-london-college-of-news-photo/2015837361">Yui Mok/PA Images via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In 2021 and 2022, major retailers and fashion brands were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretconser.2023.103413">racing into the metaverse</a>, opening virtual stores, creating digital products and inviting consumers to <a href="https://www.retaildive.com/news/retailers-connecting-metaverse-roblox-real-world-revenue/636209/">explore branded worlds</a> through avatars. Much of that excitement has since faded. But the technologies behind those experiments are <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-21/zalando-zara-use-ai-virtual-try-ons-to-tackle-clothing-returns">far from disappearing</a>.</p>

<p>Today, shoppers can try on clothes virtually, see how furniture would look in their homes and explore branded worlds on gaming platforms. Rather than building entirely new virtual universes, retailers are finding ways to integrate immersive technologies into familiar shopping experiences.</p>

<p>A 2025 global survey found that 53% of surveyed retail professionals <a href="https://cloudinary.com/blog/cloudinary-survey-results-reshaping-retail">focused on virtual fitting rooms</a>, while 46% said they were building augmented reality and virtual reality experiences. On the consumer side, a 2024 survey of more than 2,200 U.S. shoppers found that <a href="https://corporate.walmart.com/content/dam/corporate/documents/newsroom/2024/07/23/adaptive-retail-report-2024.pdf">49% of respondents would buy more clothing</a> if a great virtual try-on experience were available. Meanwhile, <a href="https://www.emarketer.com/content/shoppers-aren-t-buying-virtual-try-ons">a separate survey</a> found that only 4.5% of U.S. digital shoppers regularly used these technologies for shopping.</p>

<p>Immersive technologies continue to attract interest, but their regular use in online shopping remains limited. So what makes an immersive shopping experience worth using? </p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://experts.okstate.edu/june.park">scholar of retail and consumer sciences</a> who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=IoRKq14AAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">studies consumers’ interactions with technology</a> in the retail environment. My research suggests that the value of immersive retail isn’t simply about how advanced or realistic the technology is. It’s about how the experience is designed, how it addresses consumers’ needs and how it helps them connect with products and brands.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a computer graphic shows a male avatar standing on a virtual street lined with fashion brand imagery" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/774050/original/file-20261124-62-i737xb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Metaverse shopping, like this Metaverse Fashion Week from 2022, may be a thing of the past, but immersive shopping lives on.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/general-view-of-the-metaverse-fashion-week-on-march-25-2022-news-photo/1387688648">Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Helping shoppers see what they cannot imagine</h2>

<p>Imagine shopping for a pair of sunglasses online. You like the style, but you’re not sure how they would look on you. Amazon allows shoppers to <a href="https://sell.amazon.com/tools/3d-ar?mons_sel_locale=en_US">try on certain shoes and eyewear virtually</a> using their smartphones. IKEA applies a <a href="https://www.ikea.com/us/en/home-design/">similar concept to home furnishings</a> through IKEA Kreativ, which allows customers to digitally remove existing furniture from their rooms and experiment with new arrangements. </p>

<p>These experiences address a fundamental limitation of online shopping: the gap between seeing a product on a screen and imagining how it would look on you or in your own space.</p>

<p>My colleagues and I found that the experience of virtually trying on clothes can be particularly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/JRIM-01-2024-0015">helpful for shoppers</a> who struggle to imagine how clothing would look on them. By making it easier to visualize themselves wearing a product, the technology can help them feel more comfortable with their purchase decisions. In other words, the value of immersive technology may lie less in creating a sense of novelty than in helping consumers overcome the limitations of conventional online shopping.</p>

<h2>More personalization isn’t always better</h2>

<p>As artificial intelligence advances, so-called virtual try-on experiences are becoming increasingly personalized. Shoppers can now see clothing on digital representations of themselves rather than relying solely on images of fashion models. It might seem intuitive that the more closely a virtual model resembles a shopper, the better the experience. But our research <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2655928">suggests otherwise</a>.</p>

<p>In two experiments, we found that consumers’ responses to personalized avatars depend on what psychologists call “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(03)01005-0">assessment orientation</a>,” or the tendency to critically evaluate and compare options before making a decision. This mindset of carefully thinking through a decision can also shift depending on the shopping situation, such as choosing an outfit for a job interview versus casually browsing for fun. </p>

<p>Shoppers with a stronger evaluative mindset, whether due to their personal tendencies or the shopping situation, felt a stronger sense that they were the model and expressed greater intentions to buy when using personalized 3D avatars than when viewing conventional model images. Interestingly, the opposite pattern emerged among shoppers who are less inclined to mull over options.</p>

<p>The implication is that the same technology can offer different value to different consumers. A highly personalized experience may be particularly useful to someone who wants to thoroughly evaluate a product, but it isn’t necessarily better for everyone or every shopping situation.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/d4NN--CAi7o?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">IKEA Kreativ is an AI app from the Swedish multinational retailer that lets you virtually try out furniture in your living spaces.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>When shopping becomes more than buying</h2>

<p>Immersive technologies can also offer value beyond helping consumers decide what to buy. </p>

<p>Walmart, for example, has created <a href="https://content-naf.emarketer.com/how-walmart-turning-roblox--creators--community-marketing-engine">branded experiences on Roblox</a>, where users can explore virtual spaces, play games and discover digital products. These experiences offer retailers a new way to connect with younger consumers and build brand engagement through entertainment rather than traditional advertising. Its <a href="https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2023/09/26/walmarts-new-virtual-experience-walmart-discovered-is-inspired-by-the-community">Walmart Discovered</a> Roblox gaming environment has attracted <a href="https://content-naf.emarketer.com/how-walmart-turning-roblox--creators--community-marketing-engine">nearly 40 million visits</a> as of May 2026.</p>

<p>My research on branded virtual worlds suggests that simply creating a virtual space isn’t enough to engage consumers. What matters is how brands bring these spaces to life <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2024.108505">through storytelling and social experiences</a> that help consumers feel more connected to the brand. The value of these environments lies less in their 3D graphics than in the opportunities they create for consumers to participate, interact and become part of a brand’s story.</p>

<h2>Beyond the technology</h2>

<p>Advances in AI will likely open up even more possibilities for immersive online shopping, from more realistic virtual try-on to interactive environments that adapt to individual preferences. But making an experience more technologically sophisticated doesn’t automatically make it more valuable. </p>

<p>Whether a retailer’s goal is to help shoppers visualize products, make more informed decisions or build connections with brands, they are more likely to be successful if they design experiences around consumers rather than around the capabilities of the technology.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297364/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
